title: Regional routing cost & latency heatmap - notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working notes doc from an intra-team spike measuring how different automated routing policies affect tail latency and cost across regions. Goal: produce a compact heatmap + short recommendations to feed into the routing policy RFC (next week). Focus: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and normalized cost-per-1M-tokens for common request shapes.

Motivation:
- Customers want both low latency and low cost; routing by region/price/latency currently uses a simple score. We need empirical tradeoffs to shape the score function.
- Key question: when should we route a request off-region (cheaper model/hardware) vs. keep local (lower RTT but higher infra cost)?

Methodology (short):
- Workloads: 3 synthetic workload classes chosen to approximate real app mixes:
  1) short-chat: prompt 32 tokens, generation 64 tokens (median use case)
  2) assistant-long: prompt 256 tokens, gen 512 tokens (longer single-shot calls)
  3) embedding-batch: 128 items of 768-dim embeddings (vector workload)
- Models & variants: redwood-v1-7b (q4_0) on A100, redwood-v1-13b (q4_0) on H100, redwood-mini-2.7b (q4_0) on T4-equivalent (for cost-favored variant)
- Regions: us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1, ap-northeast1 (measured from client proxies in each region)
- Policies tested:
  A) latency-first (prefer lowest predicted p95 latency; fallback to cheapest compatible variant only if >500ms extra)
  B) cost-first (prefer lowest estimated cost; route off-region to cheaper hardware if cost delta > 20%)
  C) region-preference (sticky: prefer same-region unless capacity < 50%
  D) balanced-score (0.6*latency_norm + 0.4*cost_norm)
- Measurements: p50/p95/p99 latency observed at server-side (end-to-end), tokens/sec (aggregate), normalized infra cost per 1M tokens (USD, relative to baseline running 7b A100 in-region). Each test ran 30m steady-state with Poisson arrival matching target QPS.

Raw aggregated table (excerpt):

Columns: region | policy | workload | p50_ms | p95_ms | p99_ms | tokens_per_sec | cost_per_1M_tokens_usd

us-west1 | latency-first | short-chat | 48 | 110 | 220 | 12,400 | $1000
us-west1 | cost-first    | short-chat | 72 | 180 | 410 | 10,800 | $700
us-west1 | balanced-score| short-chat | 55 | 130 | 260 | 11,900 | $920

eu-west1 | latency-first | short-chat | 60 | 140 | 300 | 11,000 | $1020
eu-west1 | cost-first    | short-chat | 95 | 260 | 600 | 8,200  | $680

ap-northeast1 | latency-first | short-chat | 70 | 160 | 340 | 10,500 | $980
ap-northeast1 | cost-first    | short-chat | 120 | 310 | 720 | 7,300  | $660

us-west1 | latency-first | assistant-long | 120 | 290 | 640 | 3,200 | $2800
us-west1 | cost-first    | assistant-long | 200 | 480 | 1100 | 2,100 | $1700

eu-west1 | latency-first | assistant-long | 150 | 360 | 760 | 2,900 | $2950
ap-northeast1 | latency-first | assistant-long | 170 | 400 | 850 | 2,600 | $2700

embedding-batch | cost-first tends to consolidate to cheapest region/hardware giving highest throughput but adds 100-200ms extra network overhead per batch on average.

Heatmap synthesis (normalized numbers):
- For each (region, policy) we compute a 2D point (p95_ms normalized to baseline 1000, cost_per_1M normalized to baseline 1.0). Lower-left = good (low latency low cost).

Example normalized points (p95_norm, cost_norm) short-chat:
- us-west1 latency-first: (0.11, 1.00)
- us-west1 cost-first:    (0.18, 0.70)
- eu-west1 latency-first: (0.14, 1.02)
- ap-northeast1 cost-first:(0.31, 0.66)

Textual heatmap (short-chat p95 vs cost):
Rows: regions, Cols: policies (latency-first / balanced / cost-first) -> format p95_ms | cost_per_1M
- us-west1: latency-first 110ms | $1000  ; balanced 130ms | $920 ; cost-first 180ms | $700
- eu-west1: latency-first 140ms | $1020 ; balanced 170ms | $880 ; cost-first 260ms | $680
- ap-northeast1: latency-first 160ms | $980 ; balanced 220ms | $820 ; cost-first 310ms | $660

Key observations (short-chat):
- cost-first saves ~30% infra cost at the expense of increasing p95 by ~60–80ms across regions vs latency-first.
- balanced-score gives ~30% of the cost savings while only adding ~20–40ms to p95 vs latency-first.
- for short-chat, network RTT dominates when routing off-region; routing to cheapest region is only attractive if the app tolerates ~150–200ms extra p95.

Key observations (assistant-long):
- Longer generation amplifies server-side compute cost so cross-region savings are smaller as a fraction of total latency; compute dominates over RTT for assistant-long.
- cost-first still reduces cost (~30–40%) by using cheaper hardware, but adds larger p95 degradation (150–200ms) because queuing and batching mismatch on cheaper instances causes additional tail spikes.

Energy / cost note:
- Rough mapping used: A100-large per-hour cost = baseline. T4/cheap-instance variants have 0.35x running cost per token but ~1.2x token latency for medium/long sequences due to slower kernels. This was used to compute cost_per_1M_tokens_usd above.

Guidance draft for routing score (proposed):
- If predicted response size < 128 tokens (short-chat): allow cost-first routing if estimated p95 delta <= 150ms for that client region and policy. Favor balanced-score for consumer apps wanting moderate latency.
- If predicted response size >= 256 tokens: favor latency-first unless cost delta > 45% and SLA is not strict.
- Embedding-batch: default to cost-first but apply per-batch size heuristics (if batch size < 32, prefer same-region).

Operational notes and caveats:
- These tests used synthetic Poisson arrivals; real customer traffic exhibits diurnal bursts and sticky sessions that change queuing behavior.
- We observed that cheaper instance classes had higher variance under bursty arrivals; the p99 effects are amplified. Consider circuit-breaker to prevent routing to cheap-variant during load spikes.
- Measurements included only single model family; cross-model validation (llama2 / open weights) needs to be added.

Next steps (practical):
- Run a canary (2 weeks) with balanced-score in us-west and eu-west for short-chat endpoints to validate user-visible latency and cost impact.
- Add more realistic traffic traces (from customers A/B) to the benchmark harness and re-run for 72h.
- Instrument routing decisions with per-request labels so we can backfill cost + latency tradeoffs in observability dashboards.

Questions for sync:
- Thresholds: is 150ms p95 delta acceptable as a default for consumer-facing chat? (product to weigh UX)
- Should we expose TTL for region stickiness to influenced by third-party CDNs?
